parts.problem_md:
Tom is tiling a floor. The floor is a rectangle with length 600 cm and width 240 cm Each tile is a square with side 40 cm Tom uses this method to work out the number of tiles he needs. | Number of tiles that will fit along the length = 600 ÷ 40
= 15
Number of tiles that will fit along the width = 240 ÷ 40
= 6
Total number of tiles needed = 15 + 6
= 21 | |---| Give a reason why Tom’s method is wrong.
parts.solution_md: **He is correct that 15 tiles will fit along the length of the floor, and 6 tiles will fit along the width of the floor, however this would only give one line of tiles along the length, and one line of tiles along the width. He also needs to fill in the middle of the floor! The correct calculation is 15×6=90 tiles** **[1]**

parts.problem_md:
Find the area of a regular hexagon with side length 7.4 cm.

.......................................... cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solution_md:
> *Sketch a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon can be divided into 6 equilateral triangles as below.*

![V7E1R7Fr_cie-igcse-2020-may-jun-tz1-p2-q21](assets/003-v7e1r7fr-cie-igcse-2020-may-jun-tz1-p2-q21.png)

*The side lengths of the triangles are all 7.4 cm and the angles inside the triangles are all 60°* 
*We can find the area of one triangle using the sine area rule, Area *$=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are adjacent sides and *$C$* is the included angle*

$\begin{gathered} \text{Area} \Delta & = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 7.4 \times 7.4 \times \sin 60 \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply by 6 to find the area of the hexagon*

$\begin{gathered} \text{Area} \text{hexagon} & = 6 \times 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 7.4 \times 7.4 \times \sin 60 \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

$\begin{gathered} = 3 \times 7.4^{2} \times \sin 60 \\ = 142.2706533... \end{gathered}$

> *Round your answer to at least 3 significant figures*

**142 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** **** ****[1]**

equations.alt: equals 1 half a b sin C

parts.problem_md:
The sides of an isosceles triangle are measured correct to the nearest millimetre. 
One side has a length of 8.2 cm and another has a length of 9.4 cm.

Find the largest possible value of the perimeter of this triangle.

............................................ cm
parts.solution_md:
> *The largest possible value will be given by finding the upper bounds of the triangle, when the two equal sides are the longer of the given side lengths.*

> *The sides of the triangle have been rounded to the nearest millimetre, so the upper bound can be found by adding half a millimeter (0.05 cm) to the value given for each of the sides.*

> *Find the upper bound for the shorter side of the triangle.*

*Upper bound:  *$8.2+0.05=8.25$

> *Find the upper bound for the longer side of the triangle.*

*Upper bound:  *$9.4+0.05=9.45$

** ***Either upper bound calculated correctly*** ****[1]**

> *Find the largest possible value for the perimeter by adding the upper bounds for two of the longer sides and one of the shorter sides. *

*Greatest possible perimeter = 2(9.45) + 8.25*

**[1]**

**  ****Greatest possible perimeter = 27.15 cm ****[1]**

equations.alt: 8.2 space plus space 0.05 space equals space 8.25
9.4 space plus space 0.05 space equals space 9.45

parts.problem_md:
![q20-4ma1-2h-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths](assets/004-q20-4ma1-2h-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

The diagram shows a shaded region $T$ formed by removing an equilateral triangle$PQR$from a regular hexagon $ABCDEF$.

The points $P$ and $Q$ lie on $AB$ such that $AB=1.5\timesPQ$.

Given that the area of region $T$ is $72\sqrt{3}\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ work out the length of $PQ$.

......................................................$\mathrm{cm}$
parts.solution_md:
> *The formula for a triangle is *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$* where **a **and **b **are the lengths of two sides that form angle **C**.** *
*Let **x** denote the length **PQ**. Triangle **PQR** is an equilateral triangle so all the lengths are equal and all the angles are 60°. Find the area by substituting **a** = **x**, **b** = **x **and **C** = 60. Simplify the expression,*

`| Area of P Q R | = 1 half x x x x x sin ( 60 ) | | _ = 1 half x x x x x (sqrt( 3)/(2) | | _ = (sqrt( 3)/(4) x ^2 | |`

**[1]**

> *The length **PQ** = 1.5**x**.A regular hexagon is made up of 6 equilateral triangles. Find the area of the hexagon by finding substituting **a** = 1.5**x**, **b** = 1.5**x** and **C** = 60 into the formula and multiplying by 6.*

`| Area of A B C D E F | = 1 half x 1.5 x x 1.5 x x sin ( 60 ) x 6 | | _ = 1 half x 1.5 x x 1.5 x x (sqrt( 3)/(2) x 6 | | _ = (27 sqrt( 3)/(8) x ^2 | |`

**[1]**

> *Form an equation using the fact that the difference between the area of the triangle and the hexagon is equal to *$72\sqrt{3}$* cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{27 \sqrt{3} }{8} x^{2} - \frac{ \sqrt{3} }{4} x^{2} & = 72 \sqrt{3} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides √3 and multiply both sides by 8. Then solve the equation to find **x **(which is a positive value so you can ignore the negative square root).*

$\begin{array}{ccc}27 x ^{2} - 2 x ^{2} & = 576 \\ 25 x ^{2} & = 576 \\ x ^{2} & = & \frac{576}{25} \\ x = & \sqrt{\frac{576}{25}} \\ x = & \frac{24}{5}\end{array}$

**The length of ****PQ**** is 4.8 cm ****[1]**

equations.alt: A B C D E F

parts.problem_md:
A rectangle measures 8.5 cm by 10.7 cm, both correct to 1 decimal place.

Calculate the upper bound of the perimeter of the rectangle.

............................................ cm
parts.solution_md:
> *The upper bound of the perimeter of the rectangle can be calculated from the upper bounds of the length and the width of the rectangle.*

> *The length and the width have been rounded 1 decimal place (0.1), so the upper bounds can be found by adding half of 0.1 (0.05 cm) to the values given.*

> *Find the upper bound for the length.*

$10.7+0.05=10.75$

> *Find the upper bound for the width.*

$8.5+0.05=8.55$

*1 mark for either correct***  ****[1]**

> *Find the upper bound of the perimeter by adding two of the upper bounds for the lengths to two of the upper bounds for the widths.*

$\mathrm{P} = 2 ( 10.75 ) + 2 ( 8.55 )$

* **Correct method*** ****[1] **

**Upper bound of perimeter = 38.6 cm**** [1]**

equations.alt: 10.7 space plus space 0.05 space equals space 10.75
8.5 space plus space 0.05 space equals space 8.55

parts.problem_md:
The area of a square is 42.5 cm<sup>2</sup>, correct to the nearest 0.5 cm<sup>2</sup>.

Calculate the lower bound of the length of the side of the square.

.......................................... cm
parts.solution_md:
> *"Correct to the nearest" means this is a bounds question Work out the lower and upper bounds of 42.5 by adding and subtracting half of 0.5*

*Lower bound: *$42.5-\frac{1}{2}\times0.5=42.25$

*Upper bound: *$42.5+\frac{1}{2}\times0.5=42.75$

*Lower bound correct*** [1]**

> *The length of a square is the square root of its area Find the bounds of the length of a square (by square-rooting the values above)*

* *$\begin{array}{rcl} \sqrt{42.25} & = 6.5 \\ \sqrt{42.75} & = 6.538... \end{array}$

> *Write down the lower bound (by choosing the lowest value)*

**6.5 cm**** ****[1] **

**This question can be done without upper bounds**

![cie-igcse-2020-oct-nov-p4-tz1-q4b](assets/007-cie-igcse-2020-oct-nov-p4-tz1-q4b.png)

*ABDF *is a parallelogram and *BCDE  *is a straight line. *AF* = 12cm, *AB *= 9 cm, angle *CFD *= 40° and angle *FDE* = 80°.

i) Calculate the height, $h$, of the parallelogram.

$h=$ ........................................... cm [2]

ii) Calculate the area of the **trapezium ***ABCF*.

.......................................... cm<sup>2</sup> [3]
parts.solution_md:
i) *ABDF **is a parallelogram so **DF **= **AB **= 9 cm.*
*DEF ** is a right-angled triangle so right-angled trigonometry (SOHCAHTOA) can be used to find the height, **h**.*
*The hypotenuse and the angle opposite the height are known, so use the sin ratio.*

> *  *

$\mathrm{sin}θ=\frac{\mathrm{Opp}}{\mathrm{Hyp}}\,\mathrm{sin}80^{\circ}=\frac{h}{9}$

**[1]**

**   **

> *Solve by multiplying both sides by 9.  *

$\begin{gathered} 9 \sin 80^{\circ} & = h \\ h & = 9 \sin 80^{\circ} \\ = 8.86326... \end{gathered}$

$h=8.86$* ***cm (3 s.f.) ****[1]**

ii) *Method 1*

> *The formula for the area of a trapezium is *$\frac{( a + b ) h}{2}$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the parallel sides and **h** is the vertical height. *

> * Find **BC.*

*Triangle ***CDF  ***is isosceles so ***CD ***= ***DF*** = 9 cm. *

**BC = BD - CD*** = 12 - 9 = 3 cm*

**[1]**

**   **

> * Substitute into the formula for the area of a trapezium.    *

*Area ***ABCF *** =  *$\frac{( 12 + 3 ) \times 8.86326...}{2} = 66.4744...$* *

** *** **Correct method*** ****[1]**

**Area of trapezium ****ABCF****  = 66.5 cm**<sup>**2 **</sup>**[1]**

> *Method 2** *

> *The area of trapezium **ABCF  **is equal to the area of parallelogram **ABDF **minus the area of triangle **CDF**.*

> * Find the area **ABDF **using the formula area of a parallelogram = base × vertical height. Use the unrounded answer for the height found in part (i).*

* **Area ***ABDF *** = 12 × 8.86326... = 106.3592...*

> *  Find **CD.*

*Triangle ***CDF  ***is isosceles so ***CD ***= ***DF*** = 9 cm. *

**[1]*** *

> *Find the area of **CDF  **using the area of a triangle *$=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}θ$*, where *$θ$* is angle between **a **and **b**.  *

*Area ***CDF *** = *$1 \frac{1}{2} ( 9 ) ( 9 ) \sin 100^{\circ} = 39.8847...$

* **Find the area of the trapezium by subtracting area **CDF**  from area **ABDF .*

* ** **Area ***ABCF *** = 106.3592... - 39.8847... = 66.4744...*

* **Correct method ***[1]**

**Area of trapezium ****ABCF****  = 66.5 cm**<sup>**2 **</sup>**[1]**
